## Time Series Analysis

**Time series analysis** is the study of describing, modeling and forecasting
data recorded sequentially over time. Unlike in the i.i.d. setting, the
ordering of the observations carries information and successive values are
typically dependent. The field rests on a small set of core ideas:

1. Reducing a dependent sequence to a **stationary** process (by differencing,
   decomposition or transformation) so that classical asymptotic theory
   applies.

2. Characterizing dependence through the **autocovariance and autocorrelation
   functions** in the time domain, or the **spectral density** in the
   frequency domain.

3. Building parsimonious generative models (AR, MA, ARMA and their many
   descendants) whose parameters can be estimated and whose structure gives
   interpretable, testable predictions.

4. Using the fitted model to **forecast**, filter and quantify uncertainty out
   of sample.

Classical (Box-Jenkins) time series analysis focuses on the conditional
*mean* of a process and its linear dependence structure. Quantitative finance
adds a second axis that is largely absent from the classical treatment:
modeling the conditional *variance* of financial returns (volatility
clustering, leverage effects). Means are close to unpredictable, but variances
are highly persistent and directly priced, for example in options and risk
management. See [[financial-time-series]].

## Time Series

:::{.definition data-title="Time Series"}

A **time series** is a set of observations $x_t$, each recorded at a specific
time $t$. The set of observation times is denoted $T_0$.

:::

A **discrete-time** time series is one in which the set $T_0$ of observation
times is discrete, for example $T_0=\{1,\dots,n\}$ for daily closing prices.

A **continuous-time** time series is one in which observations are recorded
continuously over some time interval, such as $T_0=[0,1]$.

The examples below show both kinds.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
source("../assets/payoff-plots.R")
set.seed(1)
t_d <- 1:50
rw <- cumsum(rnorm(50))
t_c <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 500)
bm <- cumsum(rnorm(500, sd = 1 / sqrt(500)))
xt <- "x<tspan dy=\"5\" font-size=\"11\">t</tspan>"
payoff_carousel("carousel-series", list(
  series_slide("Discrete time",
    "A random walk observed at \\(t=1,\\dots,50\\).",
    t_d, rw, points = TRUE, ylab = xt),
  series_slide("Continuous time",
    "A continuous path observed on \\(T_0=[0,1]\\).",
    t_c, bm, ylab = "x(t)")
))
```

## Stationary Processes

Stationarity is a relaxation of the assumption that the random variables are
independent and identically distributed, which is often too strong.

:::{.definition data-title="Strong Stationarity"}

A real-valued stochastic process $\{X(t),~t \geq 0\}$ is **strongly
stationary** if its finite-dimensional distributions are invariant under
time shifts, that is

$$
\mathbb{P}(X(t_{1})\in B_{1}, \dots , X(t_{n})\in B_{n})
=\mathbb{P}(X(t_{1}+h) \in B_{1}, \dots , X(t_{n}+h)\in B_{n})
$$

for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $t_{1}, \dots, t_{n}\geq 0$,
$B_{1}, \dots, B_{n}\in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ and $h>0$.

:::

This is often challenging to show in practice, so a weaker form of
stationarity is defined as follows.

:::{.definition data-title="Weak Stationarity"}

A real-valued stochastic process $\{X(t),~t\geq 0\}$ with
$\mathbb{E}[X(t)^2]<\infty$ is **weakly stationary** (also known as covariance
stationary or second-order stationary) if

1. $\mu(t)=\mathbb{E}[X(t)]$ is constant on $[0,\infty)$; and

2. $\text{Cov}(X(t_{1}), X(t_{2}))=\text{Cov}(X(t_{1}+h),X(t_{2}+h))$ for every
   $t_{1}, t_{2}\geq 0$ and $h>0$.

:::

A process $X(t)$ is weakly stationary if its mean is constant and the
covariance between $t_1$ and $t_2$ depends only on the difference
$t_{2}-t_{1}$. This defines the **autocovariance function** of $X(t)$,

$$
\gamma(t_{2}-t_{1})=\text{Cov}(X(t_{1}),X(t_{2})).
$$

Strong stationarity implies weak stationarity (when second moments are
finite). The converse is not true in general, since the first and second
moments do not determine the probability distribution uniquely.

:::{.definition data-title="Stationary Gaussian Process"}

A stochastic process $\{X(t),~t \in \mathbb{R}\}$ is a **stationary Gaussian
process** if every finite-dimensional distribution of $X(\cdot)$ is Gaussian
and the process is strongly stationary.

:::

If every finite-dimensional distribution is Gaussian, that is, jointly normal,
then weak stationarity implies strong stationarity, because the joint
distribution of a finite number of normal random variables is uniquely
determined by the mean vector and covariance matrix.

The **autocorrelation function** $\rho(\cdot)$ of a weakly stationary process
$X(\cdot)$ is

$$
\rho(t)=\frac{\text{Cov}(X(t),X(0))}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X(t))\,\text{Var}(X(0))}}
=\frac{\gamma(t)}{\gamma(0)},
\qquad t \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

The three series below illustrate the definition. Only the first is
stationary. The second has a time-varying mean (a drift) and the third has a
time-varying variance (heteroscedasticity), so each violates weak
stationarity.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
source("../assets/payoff-plots.R")
set.seed(3)
t <- 1:100
xt <- "x<tspan dy=\"5\" font-size=\"11\">t</tspan>"
payoff_carousel("carousel-stationarity", list(
  series_slide("Stationary",
    "Gaussian white noise: constant mean and variance, no dependence.",
    t, rnorm(100), points = TRUE, ylab = xt),
  series_slide("Drift",
    "A linear trend plus noise: the mean \\(0.05t\\) depends on \\(t\\).",
    t, 0.05 * t + rnorm(100), points = TRUE, ylab = xt),
  series_slide("Heteroscedasticity",
    "The variance grows with \\(t\\): here \\(\\mathrm{Var}(X_t)=(t/25)^2\\).",
    t, (t / 25) * rnorm(100), points = TRUE, ylab = xt)
))
```

## White Noise

:::{.definition data-title="White Noise"}

A time series $\{Z_t\}$ is **white noise**, denoted $Z_t \sim WN(0,\sigma^2)$,
if

1. $\mathbb{E}[Z_t] = 0$ for all $t$,

2. $\mathbb{E}[Z_t^2] = \sigma^2 < \infty$ for all $t$, and

3. $\gamma_Z(h) = \text{Cov}(Z_t, Z_{t+h}) = 0$ for all $h \neq 0$.

:::

If in addition the $Z_t$ are independent and identically distributed we write
$Z_t \sim IID(0,\sigma^2)$, and if they are jointly Gaussian,
$Z_t \sim GWN(0,\sigma^2)$. White noise is the fundamental "innovation" or
"shock" process from which [[moving-average-processes|MA]],
[[autoregressive-processes|AR]] and [[arma-processes|ARMA]] models are built.

Every white noise process is weakly stationary with mean $0$ and constant
("white") spectral density $f(u) = \sigma^2/2\pi$ across all frequencies. See
[[spectral-distributions]].
